edges.effect_quant: In a 17-week randomized Stanford trial with 18 participants per arm, a high-fermented-food diet steadily increased microbiota diversity while reducing inflammatory markers, whereas a high-fiber diet did not raise diversity over the same period.
edges.population: generally healthy adults consuming fermented foods or fermented dairy products
edges.mechanism: Fermented foods can repeatedly introduce live microbes and fermentation-derived metabolites that temporarily reshape microbial community structure, expand ecological niches, and influence immune tone. The diversity effect appears strongest with sustained intake and may depend on host baseline ecology and the specific fermented foods consumed.
edges.summary: Fermented foods have one of the cleaner human signals for increasing microbiome diversity, especially when intake is sustained over weeks. Randomized diet-intervention data show rising gut diversity and lower inflammatory markers, while large observational work finds consistent if more modest microbiome differences between habitual fermented-food consumers and non-consumers.
edges.caveats: Not every fermented product acts the same way, and some intervention studies show mostly transient colonization rather than durable remodeling of the endogenous community. Diversity also does not automatically equal better health, so this edge should be read as a microbiome-structure effect with supportive but not universal clinical implications.

evidence.notes: Gut-microbiota-targeted diets modulate human immune status.
